During the play they prepare for the festival, they discover a fake sales document that will lead to the demolition of the boathouse. Let curiosity, humor, and increasing risk progress together, and ensure the child protagonists' decisions are age-appropriate. Capture the sense of adventure from Tom Sawyer and write the story in the target language at the desired reading level with original characters.

entries.label: With the wandering spirit of Huckleberry Finn, let two strangers who set out to escape learn to stay for each other.
entries.brief: Two people traveling on a riverboat are moving away from their old lives for different reasons. As they look for work or shelter at the ports where they stop, an unexpected trust forms between them. Let one encounter an opportunity where they could solve their own problem by betraying the other. Take inspiration from Huckleberry Finn regarding companionship and moral choices, but do not use the historical narrative of slavery as a simplified adventure ornament.

entries.label: With the mountain freshness of Heidi, let the return home turn into a hope greater than a farewell.
entries.brief: A protagonist who has lived in the city for a long time returns for a summer to a mountain hostel that is about to close. The nature guide they meet there sees a future for the region beyond just tourism. Let the feelings of labor, scenery, and intimacy of mountain life carry the story, and do not paint the village as a flawless paradise. Take inspiration from Heidi regarding the connection to nature and belonging, and if selected for an adult reader, establish the protagonist and the relationship at an adult level.

entries.label: With the joy of Anne of Green Gables, let someone who is said to daydream too much add color to everyone's life wherever they go.
entries.brief: A young person who is not taken seriously due to their imagination starts working at a small island's local newspaper. Their first articles make the town laugh, but one story reveals a truth that the people they love do not like. Let the protagonist's warmth as well as their capacity to make mistakes and take responsibility be visible. Take inspiration from Anne's story regarding vivid observation and finding one's place, and adjust the language level without extinguishing the literary vibrancy.

entries.label: With the sincerity of Little Women, let the dreams of siblings who grew up in the same house lead them down different paths.
entries.brief: Three siblings work together for a summer to open their family's old cinema one last time. Because one wants to be an actor, one wants to stay in town, and the other wants to travel the world, the joint venture pits their different futures against each other. Let love, competition, and daily humor complement each other, and do not count any single dream as the only right option. Take inspiration from Little Women regarding family bonds and individualization, and establish the original family and natural dialogues in the target language.

entries.label: With the feeling of revival from The Secret Garden, let an abandoned place change the people who restore it.
entries.brief: A protagonist who moved to another city against their will wants to reorganize the unused courtyard of their apartment building. Those who come to help have different expectations and cannot agree on whether the garden should be a communal or commercial space. Show the transformation through the small progress of seasons, labor, and relationships, and do not solve all problems in a single happy event. Use The Secret Garden only as a reference for healing and connecting with the environment, and keep the narrative fluent at the selected language level.

entries.label: With the strong bond of White Fang, to whom would a creature that does not trust humans entrust its life?
entries.brief: A boat builder with no experience with animals takes care of a wounded dog found after a forest fire. While the dog constantly tries to escape, the builder learns that trusting it is not about forcibly owning the animal. Bring some scenes of the story closer to the creature's perceptions, but do not make animal behavior a simple copy of human thought. Take the idea of trust being built through labor from White Fang and adjust the tension according to the reader's age.

entries.label: With the power of nature in The Call of the Wild, let a protagonist torn from their accustomed life discover another life within themselves.
entries.brief: A city-dwelling search and rescue worker is assigned to work in a remote forest region for months. The task, which they initially considered a temporary job, begins to change their life choices due to the rhythm of nature and the relationship they build with their team. Let nature carry both beauty and difficulty, and do not set up city life as a worthless contrast. Take inspiration from The Call of the Wild regarding adaptation to the environment and a new sense of belonging, and tell the new protagonist's journey on their own terms.

entries.label: With the wandering spirit of Around the World in Eighty Days, let a journey where all plans are ruined turn into the most beautiful encounter of life.
entries.brief: A photographer sets out to bring together old friends living in different countries at the same exhibition. While a meticulous archivist accompanying them sees a new problem at every unplanned stop, the photographer finds a new possibility. Let lost connections and changing routes develop their relationship, and do not let the stops turn into a list of tourist information. Take the sense of movement from Verne's novel and make the travel conversations a natural part of the events in the target language.

entries.label: With the excitement of the search in In Search of the Castaways, let a clue that changes at every port take two siblings to the other end of the world.
entries.brief: Two adult siblings travel around coastal cities to document the final voyage of the research ship their mother worked on for years. While their initial goal is to prepare an exhibition, they learn about the disagreement in the final days of the voyage from different witnesses. As the research progresses, the heroic story told in the family should become more complex and human. Take the idea of tracking in a vast geography from In Search of the Castaways, and do not repeat the same rescue plot of the lost parent.

entries.label: With the longing for home in The Odyssey, is it difficult for someone who has crossed all the seas to enter their own door?
entries.brief: A woman who has worked at sea for years decides to return permanently to the port city where she grew up. She realizes that the life she expected has already changed and that her old friends attach different meanings to her return. Let memories of external journeys appear at selected moments to explain current relationships. Take the tension between return and changing identity from The Odyssey, and do not use mythological trials or the epic's events literally.

entries.label: With the power of words in Cyrano de Bergerac, let the love sentences written for someone else one day betray one's own heart.
entries.brief: A playwright is given the task of preparing the speech for a close friend's marriage proposal. While writing, they realize that their feelings are directed not toward the friend's fiancée, but toward the set designer they are rehearsing with. Let the difference between what is said and what is felt create humor and subtle dialogues, and do not reward deception as a romantic success. Take the relationship between language and emotion from Cyrano, and do not reconstruct the well-known love triangle in the same way.

entries.label: With the passion of The Black Tulip, let the dream of growing a flower take root between prohibitions and a great love.
entries.brief: A gardener tries to keep a rare plant alive in a botanical garden that reopened after the war. While getting closer to the archive officer they consulted to access specimens of the plant, they learn that the garden will be sold for another purpose. Let the growing process require real labor and let love develop within the disagreements of working together. Take the passion for creating beauty from The Black Tulip, and do not reuse the competition and imprisonment plot.

entries.label: With the playful intelligence of Arsène Lupin, let the thief everyone is looking for attend the invitation to return the stolen artifact.
entries.brief: A former art thief goes to a collector's flashy invitation to find an artifact stolen by someone else. The detective following them realizes that they are acting more reliably than most of the guests. Let mutual moves, role changes, and subtle humor carry the events, and do not base the solution on secret technology added later. Take the wit and lightness from Lupin narratives, and do not use the same protagonist or known heists.

entries.label: Leaning on the attention of Sherlock Holmes, let a detail noticed by an ordinary passenger make everyone on the ship a suspect.
entries.brief: A valuable prototype goes missing on a night ferry and must be found before reaching land. A sound technician notices that the sounds they heard on the ship do not match the order described by the witnesses. Give clues to the reader in time and make each suspect's relationship with the prototype understandable. Take the pleasure of deduction from Holmes, and do not break the logic chain by simplifying it, even if short sentences are required in the target language.

entries.label: With the wonder of Journey to the Center of the Earth, let an exploration team encounter a completely different nature where the map ends.
entries.brief: A cave research team discovers a previously unseen large underground void beneath a dried-up lake. The painter and the geologist on the team cannot agree on whether to reveal their findings to the world, as the area holds a very fragile ecosystem. Let the problems of exploration, navigation, and exiting create gripping scenes. Take the excitement of discovery from Verne's novel, and do not mix fantastic assumptions with real geology.

entries.label: With Alice's sense of curiosity, enter a city where everything is explained logically but nothing makes sense.
entries.brief: A designer visits a city with strange rules where everyone takes their job extremely seriously. They learn that permission is required to find a way in the city, and an arrival document is required to get permission. While the contradiction of the rules unfolds with humor, let the protagonist build relationships with different people to understand the city. Take the wordplay and logical confusion from Alice, and build new scenes without relying on word games that are untranslatable in the target language.

entries.label: With Gulliver's bewilderment, let the most normal habit be considered the greatest oddity in a foreign country.
entries.brief: A chef learns in the country they went to for a job application that food is evaluated by the sounds they make before their tastes. To succeed, they must first understand the reason for the tradition they mocked. Let the cultural difference surprise both sides, and do not base the comedy on belittling a single society. Take the idea of looking at habits from the outside from Gulliver, and do not make the fictional society a caricature of a real nation.

entries.label: With the joy of discovery in The Wizard of Oz, let a traveler wanting to return home find the power they seek in their companions.
entries.brief: A protagonist who boards the wrong ship in a remote region sets out with a small group to find the port to return home. Each of the travel companions encounters an obstacle where a talent they think they lack is needed. Let the solution be based on actions taken during the journey, not on a reward given by an authority figure. Take the sense of companionship and discovery from Oz, and do not repeat the characters and symbolic objects.

entries.label: With Pollyanna's hope, let someone whose optimism is underestimated be able to express their own sadness while making everyone laugh.
entries.brief: An actor who recently joined a traveling theater that has been losing money for a long time wants to revive the tour the team gave up on. The small jokes they make to encourage people work, but they also have a serious anxiety of their own. Do not frame optimism as denying all pain, and grant the protagonist the right to receive support. Take the idea of building relationships with hope from Pollyanna and describe the variety of emotions naturally in the target language.

entries.label: With the sense of justice in Oliver Twist, let the words of someone who is looked down upon shake the order of the powerful.
entries.brief: A young apprentice working in a workshop notices that their master, who constantly takes credit for the work done, is hiding the truth about an important order. If they speak up, they might lose their livelihood; if they stay silent, the other apprentices will remain under a heavier burden. Do not make solidarity form easily, and ensure the adults who help also have their limits. Take inspiration from Oliver Twist regarding the dignity of the person seen as powerless, and if a child protagonist is chosen, adjust the level of danger according to their age.

entries.label: Inspired by the perspective of The Little Prince, let the most valuable thing on a long journey be a bond that does not fit in a suitcase.
entries.brief: A botanist traveling to small settlements for duty encounters people protecting a different plant everywhere. While aiming to achieve success with the specimens they collect, they learn that some bonds disappear when removed from their place. Let intellectual depth arise from concrete encounters, and do not fill the narrative with ready-made aphorisms. Take the idea of attention and bonding from The Little Prince, and do not use the planets, characters, or famous sentences.

entries.label: Not eighty days, just one summer: let three travelers from different countries share the fate of the same boat.
entries.brief: Three people who do not know each other join the same voyage to use an old sailboat one last time before it is sold. One is focused on family heritage, one on freedom, and the other on the money they will earn. Throughout the journey, let the question of who the boat belongs to give way to the question of what they can do with it. Tell the sea adventure with lively conversations and different character voices suitable for the selected language level.

entries.label: Let a traveler learn in a city they have never seen that everyone has been waiting for them for years.
entries.brief: A musician arrives at a festival in a small border town for the first time, and people welcome them as if they kept a very old promise. They soon realize that the expected person is someone else with the same name, but the continuation of the festival depends on them taking the stage. Do not hide the mistaken identity situation artificially for a long time, and let the different consequences of telling the truth carry the story. Let the sense of humor, belonging, and finding one's place turn into a fluent adventure in the target language.

entries.label: While one wants to leave and one wants to stay, let both try to save the same island hotel.
entries.brief: Two partners managing an island hotel that will close at the end of the season work together to host their last guests. One of the partners wants to sell the business and live in another country, while the other has worked for years to be able to return to the island. Let the guests' small stories enrich the main conflict but not replace the actual decision. Establish the romantic or friendly relationship according to the sub-genre chosen by the user, and do not let the language level infantilize the characters.

entries.label: If a theater troupe goes to the wrong country, can they open the curtain without knowing any common language?
entries.brief: A touring team buys tickets to the wrong country due to two cities with similar names. They are forced to share the same stage with a local performance group they accidentally meet there. Let misunderstandings during the rehearsal process create humor, and let cooperation develop through labor and mutual curiosity. Let the narrative be entirely in the selected target language, and do not turn it into a translation exercise to explain the language barrier to the reader.

entries.label: Let two rival chefs be forced to set the same table in the most remote kitchen in the world.
entries.brief: Rivals of a cooking show are stranded in a mountain village cut off from the outside world due to a storm. They are asked to prepare food together with limited ingredients for the village's big wedding. Do not let their rivalry produce only bickering; let one be strong in technical mastery and the other in building relationships with people. Write a warm, gripping story with concrete ingredients and work scenes without using the local cuisine as mere decor.

entries.label: Let a mountaineer be forced to entrust their life to their old rival to reach the summit they have wanted to conquer for years.
entries.brief: A mountaineer sets out on the same route for the last time with their former partner, whom they accused of abandoning the team in the past. An unexpected weather change leads the two to opposing decisions regarding the return route. Let the truth of the past event be revealed along with the choices of the journey, and do not let a single explanation immediately resolve all grievances. Derive the tension from natural conditions and the test of trust, and do not solve mountaineering practices with random miracles.

entries.label: Let a musician recognize a single person in the audience in the middle of the concert that will save their entire career.
entries.brief: A young pianist sees their first teacher, whom they haven't seen for years, among the audience in the final of the big competition. They remember that the piece they used while choosing their program had wronged the teacher in the past. Let the story connect the pre-concert preparation with the moment of decision on stage, and let success on the outside conflict with responsibility on the inside. Even if the narrative is simplified according to the language level, preserve the emotional subtlety of the music and the relationship.

entries.label: If a painter becomes famous for a painting they did not make, which day would they choose to tell the truth?
entries.brief: An anonymous work exhibited in the studio of a painter struggling with financial difficulties is mistakenly thought to be their work. While they intend to correct the mistake, the painting becomes the face of the campaign that will bring a large donation to the art school that is about to close. Let the effort to find the true owner of the work conflict with the painter's own desire for success. Tell the story through art, labor, and public expectation without making it an easy lesson on confession.

entries.label: Let two friends who parted years ago try to buy the boat they lost, without each other knowing.
entries.brief: Childhood friends learn that the boat they first went to sea with together is up for sale. One comes to repair it, the other to retrieve old family belongings inside. While their encounter reopens an old disagreement, the true condition of the boat requires them to work together. Do not reduce nostalgia to only beautiful memories; let current needs and changed personalities also be visible.

entries.label: While a caravan is crossing the desert, why would the person who knows the way best want to turn back?
entries.brief: A cargo caravan sets out to cross the desert during the last safe passage of the season. The experienced guide's opposition to the new route is first mistaken for cowardice, but the guide has the consequences of a decision they made on this route in the past. Let water, distance, and in-team duties be concrete elements of the tension. Tell the knowledge and preferences of the people living there without using the geography as an exotic background.

entries.label: Let an astronomer not be alone at the telescope on the night they find the sign they have been looking for for years.
entries.brief: An astronomer at a small observatory is making their final observations before their funds are cut. A traveler who takes shelter with them that night helps not with the explanation of the signal found, but first with its verification. Let the duo's different life choices emerge in the conversations of the long wait, and investigate the scientific result without it carrying certainty. Combine the excitement of discovery with human closeness, and provide explanations in the target language only as much as the event requires.

entries.label: Let a marine biologist find their childhood sweetheart's new port project in the bay they are trying to save.
entries.brief: A marine biologist returns to the coast where they grew up years later to protect a sensitive breeding area. The person managing the port project is their former lover, and they sincerely believe it will create jobs in the town. Do not tie the conflict between the environment and the need for livelihood to a one-sided villain; let both protagonists have their data and blind spots. Build an original narrative that develops romantic tension along with professional choices.

entries.label: Let a traveling librarian hear the ending of their own novel that they never wrote in the last village they bring books to.
entries.brief: A writer working as a traveling librarian learns that the novel they left unfinished years ago has turned into an oral narrative. People in the village have given their protagonist a different ending and associated this ending with a real event. While the writer wants to regain control of their narrative, they begin to see the value of the story changing among people. Write a curious story about literature, ownership, and collective imagination without requiring a supernatural secret.

entries.label: If two translators have published the same book with different endings, who will find the author's lost voice?
entries.brief: Two translators gain fame by using different final pages of the same travel diary. When they are sent to research together for the new edition of the work, they realize that both texts belong to another period. Let their rivalry progress with document examinations, interviews with witnesses, and confrontations regarding their own preferences. Keep the entire narrative for the reader in the selected target language, and do not let professional details stifle the naturalness of the dialogues.

entries.label: Before an archaeologist announces their great discovery, let them be forced to answer a question from a child visiting the excavation site.
entries.brief: An archaeologist is preparing a press conference, thinking they have found a structure that has been sought for many years. A local child asking why certain stones look new requires the team to re-examine their assumption. Show the value of daily observation in research without making the child a genius who knows all science. Let the conflict of discovery, prestige, and the ability to admit mistakes turn into an adventure suitable for the age group in the target language.

entries.label: Let a photographer begin to get to know a city that does not appear in any of their photographs.
entries.brief: A photographer who comes to the city only to take photos of flashy buildings meets an old bicycle repairman who tells about the back streets. The repairman does not take them to invisible magical places, but to the lives of the people they constantly leave out of their photos. As the protagonist's perspective changes, let their work conflict with the responsibility of the relationship they build with people. Use visual details selectively and make the story a true narrative of change instead of a travel guide.

entries.label: When a space courier makes their last delivery, let them learn that the shipment is not a package but a farewell.
entries.brief: A courier making small deliveries between planets takes an old instrument to an elderly musician in a remote colony before quitting the job. The package also carries the last joint concert request of a friend they haven't heard from in years. If the courier chooses the journey that will bring the two together, they might miss their last ship connection. Make the science fiction environment lively with daily life, and tell the emotional conflict without turning it into a great universe secret.

entries.label: While everyone is playing a role at a historical ball, let the only person who is not in disguise hide the most things.
entries.brief: At the first grand ball of a newly established republic, a young journalist investigates the past identities of the guests. A tailor who comes openly under their own name carries more information about the most important politician of the night than anyone else. Let the intrigue progress with class differences, friendships, and interests, and let the identity games leave understandable traces. Let the historical period and country be chosen in a way that suits the user's preferences, and do not attribute fake crimes to real people.

entries.label: When a pastry chef receives their biggest order, let them learn why the wedding was held in secret.
entries.brief: A chef trying to keep their small pastry shop afloat receives a large order for a wedding in a remote country house. During the preparation, it is understood that the reason is not family conflict, but that one of them is looking for an opportunity to make a decision together before an unexpected journey. Let the faltering details of the ceremony create humor and intimacy, and let the protagonist's own postponements in their life also be visible. Build the warm narrative not with simple coincidences, but with small but difficult decisions made by the characters.

entries.label: As an orchestra conductor begins to lose their hearing, let them decide to whom they will entrust their last concert.
entries.brief: An experienced orchestra conductor is preparing for the season's last concert when they notice the change in their hearing. Their talented assistant is ready to support, but the conductor experiences handing over the task as losing their entire identity. Do not solve the health condition with a miraculous treatment, and tell the process of different working methods and accepting help. Even if the reader's language level is low, preserve the protagonist's adult emotional conflict.

entries.label: When roads are closed in a winter village, let two families who are at odds be forced to light the same oven.
entries.brief: In a village cut off from the outside due to heavy snow, only the old communal oven is in working condition. Two families who have not been able to agree on the ownership of the oven for years are forced to share fuel and division of labor. Let the characters' humor, old grievances, and daily craftsmanship create warm scenes. Do not count reconciliation as an automatic result, and show which problem working together solves and which it leaves open.

entries.label: When a traveler returns with the wrong suitcase, let an unfinished life come out of it instead of money.
entries.brief: A port worker finds the materials of an incomplete puppet show in a suitcase mixed up after a journey. Upon reaching the owner, they learn that the artist is about to quit the tour and wants to perform the play one last time. Let the task of returning the suitcase turn into a small journey where two people change each other's lives. Derive the tension from the possibility of giving up, labor, and trying again instead of a hidden crime.

entries.label: If a rally driver reaches the finish line carrying their rival, how would the story of the race they lost be told?
entries.brief: A rally driver sees their old rival's vehicle overturned in the final stage that will determine their career. Helping might put them out of the race, but the rival's team says no other help can reach them. Do not let the public's ready-made heroic story after the race cover up the complex emotions the driver is experiencing. Tell the pressure of speed and decision with lively scenes, and do not turn safety interventions into an unrealistic individual show.

entries.label: When a puppeteer comes to a city that never laughs, let them learn to listen to people before making them laugh.
entries.brief: A traveling puppeteer is forced to stay for a few weeks in an industrial city where their shows do not find a response. While thinking that people have no sense of humor, they realize that their own plays do not see their lives at all. Let them develop their new play from conversations with market tradespeople, children, and night workers. Build a cheerful narrative about mutual recognition and the transformation of art without making the city a cursed place.

entries.label: Let a pilot recognize a passenger from their first flight years later; let both have chosen another life that day.
entries.brief: A pilot preparing for their last flight before retirement recognizes the young physician from their first voyage among the passengers. As the two talk about how the same flight created completely different beginnings in their lives, they realize that a postponed joint decision is possible again. Use past scenes when they change the meaning of today's conversation, and do not multiply coincidences one after another. Tell the feeling of journey, time, and second chances with a natural relationship in the selected target language.

entries.label: As a polar research team prepares to return home, let them learn that the ship that will take them will not come.
entries.brief: The team closing the research station at the end of the season learns that the rescue ship cannot approach for weeks due to ice conditions. Supplies are sufficient, but the hidden disagreements within the group grow during the wait. Let environmental conditions, task sharing, and communication efforts create real tension, and do not connect every chapter to the same panic scene. Give the adventure warmth and humor, and keep the technical information understandable at the reader's language level.

entries.label: While a novelist is explaining their book to a reader who has never read them, let them find the story they really wanted to write.
entries.brief: A novelist whose success is declining talks to a carpenter who does not know their works at all on a long sea voyage. As they try to explain their novels, they realize the same personal question they avoided in every book. Do not let the carpenter settle into the ready-made role of the wise man; let them participate in the relationship with their own story and objections. Let the passion for writing, fear of failure, and new beginnings be told with scenes that carry each other.

entries.label: If the last open-air cinema in a city is to close, which people, not which film, would meet at the last screening?
entries.brief: The projectionist preparing the last night of an open-air cinema invites the viewers who have sat in the same seats for years. Some come to meet an old love, some to show their child their past, and some just to say goodbye. Let different lives be connected to the question of what the main protagonist wants to do in the future, and let each encounter carry new information. Along with nostalgia, include humor, current needs, and the possibility of continuing.
